name: Thymalin

lead: Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract developed in Russia as an immune-modulating drug and promoted within a family of 'bioregulator' peptides for ageing.
Support comes mostly from animal studies and reports by its developers. It has no documented appearance use.

paras: Proponents say its thymic peptides activate T-cell differentiation and restore immune function; Thymogen (Glu-Trp) and Vilon were derived from it.
The sources reviewed do not describe human adverse effects. It is an animal-derived preparation, and legal status varies by country.

lead: Thymalin is a Russian pharmaceutical preparation made by mild acid extraction of calf thymus. It was put into practice there as an immunocorrector, a drug meant to modulate immune function.[1]

From it the same research group isolated the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, later sold as Thymogen, and designed the synthetic dipeptide Vilon.[1][2] Thymalin is also grouped with Epithalamin in the Khavinson program on peptides and ageing.[3][4] Evidence is mainly from animal and cell studies; this entry's sources include no randomized trial of Thymalin for appearance.
infobox: Prescription-type drug in Russia; research peptide elsewhere

paras: Natural thymic peptides were isolated from calf thymus by mild acid extraction, and a pharmaceutical containing them was named Thymalin.[1] The extract is a complex mixture and the group has also studied purified or synthetic components.[1][2]

Reviews from the developing group state that Thymalin and related peptides modulate immunity, and that a thymic peptide plus a pineal peptide prolonged life in older people in a long-term study.[4] The dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp derived from Thymalin is reported to have slowed ageing and inhibited spontaneous tumours in rats.[2] A 2018 paper examined Thymalin's effect on tumour and thymus under activation therapy in vivo.[5] A 2022 cell study included Thymalin among five peptides tested in THP-1 monocyte/macrophage cells.[6] An older mouse study examined thymic preparations in experimental parasite infection.[7]

Clinical reports exist mainly from the Russian developing group. One 2003 paper from that group reported that peptides of pineal gland and thymus prolonged human life;[4] its details are not reproduced here, and no independent randomized trial was found among the sources reviewed. A 1997 review describes use as an immunocorrector in practice.[1]
